analysis.one_liner: Opens the federal employee health insurance program to any American who can pay the full premium.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Oversight and Government Reform Committee until the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Darrell Issa's bill would have directed the Office of Personnel Management to contract with private insurers to sell the same health plans federal workers get to anyone not already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, or a federal program. Enrollees would pay the entire premium themselves with no government subsidy, though premiums would be tax-deductible, and their premiums would be pooled separately from federal employees so their costs could not be spread onto federal workers' plans. It was introduced in July 2009, during the debate over the Affordable Care Act, as an alternative way to cover the uninsured.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and individually insured Americans who earn too much for Medicaid but cannot get employer coverage would gain access to the large, stable Federal Employees Health Benefits pool's menu of private plans, which typically offer more plan choices and better bargaining power than the individual market. The private insurance carriers that hold FEHBP contracts would gain a new national customer base, and they could not be forced in — but OPM may condition its federal-employee contracts on carriers also serving the new pool. Higher-income enrollees get the biggest tax benefit from the new above-the-line premium deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Any individual not eligible for Medicare, Medicaid, or federal employee coverage could enroll in a Federal Employees Health Benefits plan, giving people locked out of employer coverage access to the same menu of private plans federal workers use.

OPM would have to contract each year with one or more carriers to make plans available, and it may require carriers seeking federal-employee contracts to also serve the new pool, giving OPM leverage to keep plans on offer.
Premiums would be deductible from income tax, a tax break for people buying coverage on their own.

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees themselves: the bill explicitly provides no government contribution toward premiums, so participants pay the full cost of coverage out of pocket, softened only by the tax deduction that helps higher-income filers most. Taxpayers bear the administrative cost of OPM running a second national insurance program, and any revenue cost of the new deduction.

drawbacks.text: No subsidy: the bill bars any government contribution, so people most likely to need it — those who cannot afford coverage now — would still face the full premium, and the tax deduction is worth the most to higher earners.
Premiums could vary by geographic region, so people in high-cost areas could pay substantially more for the same coverage.

The bill does not require carriers to cover people with pre-existing conditions or restrict how they price or deny coverage, unlike the ACA reforms debated at the same time; OPM applies the federal-employee rules only 'to the greatest extent practicable,' leaving open how much protection enrollees would actually get.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real coverage avenue — the FEHBP menu is a genuinely better deal than most individual markets — but without subsidies it would mainly help people who could already roughly afford insurance, and it carried none of the patient protections (guaranteed issue, community rating) that the ACA ultimately imposed. As a standalone fix for the uninsured it was weak; as a market-based alternative during the 2009 health debate it was a partisan marker.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Ways and Means Committees, sent to a subcommittee in October 2009, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on July 31, 2009, during the congressional debate over what became the Affordable Care Act.
It was referred jointly to the House Oversight and Government Reform and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction.
On October 23, 2009, it was referred to the Oversight subcommittee on the Federal Workforce, Post Office, and the District of Columbia; no further action is recorded.
The bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself. The private health insurance industry was better off because the bill died alongside the broader 2009 health debate: the ACA that passed instead subjected the individual insurance market to guaranteed-issue and medical-loss-ratio rules that the industry opposed, while this bill would simply have routed more unsubsidized customers to carriers. People who wanted the government to simply stay out of new health coverage arrangements also got the outcome they preferred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and opponents of new coverage rules

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the federal employee health plan menu to the general public.

for.name: 1 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democrat to do so.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Edolphus Towns (D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill beyond referring it to a subcommittee; it never received a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the tax provisions, chaired by Charles Rangel (D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the 111th Congress agenda
against.what_they_did: Pursued the Affordable Care Act as the vehicle for health coverage expansion and did not advance this bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was Republican-sponsored with 7 of 178 House Republicans cosponsoring; the only Democrat among 253 joined, and the Democratic majority that controlled the committees never acted on it, instead advancing the ACA.

industries.note: Carriers would gain a new national pool of full-premium customers, and OPM could condition federal-employee contracts on carriers serving the new pool — extra leverage in the insurers' most stable government line of business. But the bill imposed no new coverage mandates or guaranteed-issue rules, so insurers would take on only customers who could pay.

industries.industry: Federal employee health benefits program (OPM as administrator)
industries.note: The bill makes the FEHBP infrastructure and its contracted carriers the permanent vehicle for a new public market, though with a separate risk pool protecting federal employees from cost spillover.
